writing.explanation:
Matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] advances the Fibonacci state by one. Raising it to power 50 gives F(50)=12586269025 in the appropriate entry. The identity matrix handles exponent zero; the sample bounds keep u64 arithmetic representable.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse n and return Fibonacci F(n), with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1; n<=90 in this u64 example. The visible fixture is `n=50` and its example result is `12586269025`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Matrix Exponentiation when it asks for huge recurrence indexes and state transitions. Here the concrete task is: Parse n and return Fibonacci F(n), with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1; n<=90 in this u64 example. The visible input `n=50` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Check number size, sign, and modulus assumptions before using a shortcut; not every inverse or division exists. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Encode a linear recurrence as a matrix and exponentiate the transition by squaring. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? An arithmetic or bitwise transformation relies on an identity. Write that identity and the domain in which it holds. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(k^3 log n) time · O(k^2) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `12586269025` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test zero, one, powers of two, maximum input size, and overflow or underflow around intermediate products. Use explicit integer widths and checked arithmetic when input bounds require them. Distinguish bit positions from numeric values. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
